question: Did QWERTY survive because typists and employers locked themselves into a worse keyboard?
answer: Once typists trained on QWERTY and offices bought QWERTY machines, each side's choice bound the other and nobody could switch alone, as the economist Paul David argued. US Navy trials in the 1940s reported that retraining typists on August Dvorak's layout quickly repaid its cost. A better design lost because it arrived second.
move: Whichever side you took, whether any fair test showed the rival faster decides it.
ask: What do I call a worse habit locked in, when no fair test has ever shown the rival is better?
counterpoint: Liebowitz and Margolis traced those Navy trials to Dvorak himself, the layout's patent holder. A 1956 US government study under Earl Strong found retrained Dvorak typists no faster than QWERTY typists given the same extra training. Later tests show small gains at most. The layout that lost was never shown to be clearly better.
source: Liebowitz & Margolis, Fable of the Keys, 1990
reference: Liebowitz & Margolis, The Fable of the Keys, Journal of Law and Economics, 1990
